newsitem.title: UK: UK welcomes EMI report, sees no threat to London.
newsitem.headline: UK welcomes EMI report, sees no threat to London.

text.p: Britain on Friday welcomed the future European central bank's blueprint for monetary policy under a single European currency and bankers said they saw no threat to London's role as Europe's top financial centre.

"London remains in pole position," said one UK economist at a leading UK house. "The major battleground is where the centre for trading the euro will be and I would be confident of our position there."
The Bank of England said it welcomed "the substance" of a report by the Frankfurt-based European Monetary Institute and in particular its conclusions on monetary strategy.
But Britain could be hampered if it stayed outside European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), particularly if UK banks were denied equal access to the new cross-border bank settlement system.

The central bank was guarded in its comments on two key areas of disagreement. The suggested introduction of minimum reserve requirements for banks could be damaging, amounting to a tax on business, it said.

And on access to TARGET -- the Trans-European Automated Real-Time Gross Settlement Express Transfer system -- it merely noted that "there remains an unresolved debate" and that its views had already been made known.
Germany is unhappy about allowing countries outside EMU full access to intraday euro liquidity, fearing this will disrupt efforts to control European monetary policy.
The EMI report saidthe central banks of countries outside the single currency would not be able to extend overnight credit in the euro to institutions in their countries, adding:
"Mechanisms are being prepared to prevent intraday credit, if granted to non-euro area national central banks, from spilling over into overnight credit."
The Bank of England says all EU nations should have equal access to intraday credit and does not see this as an obstacle to the smooth conduct of monetary policy.

"It is perfectly possible to prevent any tangible spillover from the settlement system into money supply creation by imposing penalties on overnight borrowing," deputy governor Howard Davies said last October.

But Gavyn Davies, chief economist at Goldman Sachs and one of Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke's independent advisers said a European Central Bank would not look too kindly on European Union countries sitting smugly outside EMU.

"If we decide to stay outside the single currency...and essentially have a good time outside the system, then we will definitely pay a political penalty in other ways as members of the European Union," he told BBC radio.

A spokesman for the British Bankers' Association (BBA) said on Friday it still took the view that there was no economic case for distinguishing between "ins" and "outs" as far as access to intraday liquidity is concerned.

The spokesman said most of the detail in the EMI report appeared to be sound. "But the BBA will continue to press for a clear commitment to full and equal access to TARGET for "outs' as for "ins.'" If access is denied then other options would be available, he added.
Philip Shaw, chief economist at Union Plc, agreed. "It could makes thing more awkward but I suspect an alternative system could be devised to circumvent TARGET."
Banking sources say one alternative could involve developing London as an offshore centre for parallel trading in euro.
